newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Japan's Hashimoto hopes to cement Indonesia ties.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto hopes to cement Indonesia ties.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will seek to cement ties with Southeast Asia's biggest country while carefully avoiding contentious issues when he arrives in Indonesia on Thursday.
Hashimoto has no plans to raise either Indonesia's controversial national car policy or human rights in East Timor in talks with President Suharto, Japanese Ambassador Taizo Watanabe said.
Japan, the United States and the European Union have protested to the World Trade Organisation over Indonesia's car policy, which gives tax breaks to a company headed by one of Suharto's sons.

Watanabe told reporters at a pre-visit briefing the prime minister also had no intention of discussing East Timor despite calls by anti-Indonesian activist and Nobel Peace laureate Jose Ramos Horta in Tokyo this week for Japan to press Jakarta on the issue.

The ambassador said that due to the importance of relations with the region, Hashimoto had decided to go ahead with his first official tour of five Southeast Asian nations despite the crisis at home over the taking of hostages at the Japanese embassy in Peru by Marxist guerrillas.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas has welcomed the visit. "It is an important visit because Japanese-Indonesian relations are important," he said.

Hashimoto arrives in Jakarta from Malaysia at 10:30 a.m. (0330 GMT) on Thursday and leaves for Vietnam on Saturday. He is also visiting Brunei and Singapore -- all members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
He visited the other two ASEAN members, Thailand and the Philippines, last year.
Watanabe said the Japanese leader believed "maintaining and cementing close cooperation and foreign relations with Indonesia is vitally important".
He noted Japan was Indonesia's biggest trading partner and biggest aid donor. Japanese investment in Indonesia rose to nearly $7.0 billion in 1996 from $3.8 billion in 1995.
Another key element of the relationship was that 53 percent of Japan's vital imports of raw materials moved through the sea lanes of the sprawling Indonesian archipelago.
Indonesia is also Japan's third-largest foreign source of oil and natural gas.
Watanabe said Hashimoto's talks with President Suharto would extend beyond issues of bilateral interest to embrace international affairs.
The ambassador said that international problems such as the environment, contagious diseases such as AIDS and drugs were important foreign policy issues.
"This year we are trying to promote cooperation with the ASEAN region for the purpose of stability of the region and revitalising trade and investment relations," Watanabe said.
He said an eight-to-10 member task force was accompanying Hashimoto to keep the prime minister in touch with Tokyo and Lima over the Peruvian hostage crisis.
